content: 1. A child with cutaneous anthrax had no prior visible cuts, abrasions, or lesions at the site where the cutaneous lesion developed. 2. 3. Cutaneous lesions were observed on the forearm, neck, chest, and fingers. 4. The only published case report of cutaneous anthrax from the 2001 attacks highlighted the difficulty in diagnosing the disease in a previously healthy 7-month-old infant. The disease progressed rapidly to severe systemic illness despite hospitalization, with clinical manifestations including microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with renal involvement, coagulopathy, and hyponatremia. 5. Fortunately, the child recovered, and none of the cutaneous anthrax cases diagnosed after the 2001 attacks were fatal. 6. Gastrointestinal anthrax is thought to occur after the deposition and germination of spores in the upper or lower gastrointestinal tract. 7. However, due to the rapid transit time in the gastrointestinal tract, it is more likely that many cases result from the ingestion of large numbers of vegetative bacilli from poorly cooked infected meat rather than from spores. 8. The oral-pharyngeal form of gastrointestinal anthrax results in oral or esophageal ulcers, leading to regional lymphadenopathy, edema, and sepsis. 9. Disease in the lower gastrointestinal tract manifests as primary intestinal lesions, predominantly in the terminal ileum or cecum, initially presenting with nausea, vomiting, and malaise, and rapidly progressing to bloody diarrhea, acute abdomen, or sepsis. 10. By hospital day 12, a 2-cm black eschar was present in the center of the cutaneous lesion. 11. Massive ascites has been reported in some cases of gastrointestinal anthrax. 12. Advanced gastrointestinal anthrax infection may resemble the sepsis syndrome seen in inhalational or cutaneous anthrax. 13. Some authors suggest that aggressive medical intervention, as recommended for inhalational anthrax, may reduce mortality. 14. However, due to the difficulty of early diagnosis of gastrointestinal anthrax, mortality rates may be high. 15. Postmortem examinations in Sverdlovsk revealed gastrointestinal submucosal lesions in 39 of 42 patients, but all of these patients also had definitive pathological evidence of an inhalational source of infection. 16. No gastrointestinal anthrax cases were diagnosed in either the Sverdlovsk series or following the 2001 anthrax attacks. 17. 18. A patient seeking medical treatment for symptoms of inhalational anthrax is likely to be the first evidence of a clandestine release of Bacillus anthracis as a biological weapon. 19. The appearance of even a single previously healthy patient who becomes acutely ill with nonspecific febrile illness and symptoms consistent with anthrax should prompt consideration of anthrax infection. 20. Recognition of cutaneous anthrax cases may also serve as the first evidence of an anthrax attack. 21. Abnormal findings on chest X-ray or chest CT scan are diagnostically important in cases of inhalational anthrax. 22. Although anthrax does not cause classic bronchopneumonia pathologically, it can cause widened mediastinum, massive pleural effusions, air bronchograms, necrotizing pneumonic lesions, and/or consolidation. 23. These findings can result in hypoxemia and chest imaging abnormalities that may or may not be clinically distinguishable from pneumonia. 24. In the 2001 anthrax attacks, all of the first 10 patients had abnormal chest X-ray results, and all 8 patients who underwent CT scans had abnormal findings, including widened mediastinum on chest radiographs and effusions on chest CT scans. 25. Such findings in a previously healthy patient with overwhelming febrile illness or sepsis would strongly suggest advanced inhalational anthrax. 26. In advanced inhalational anthrax, the bacterial burden may be so high that bacilli are visible on Gram stain of peripheral blood, as observed in the 2001 attacks. 27. The most useful microbiologic test is the standard blood culture, which typically shows growth within 6 to 24 hours. 28. All 8 patients who had blood cultures obtained before starting antibiotics had positive blood cultures. 29. Blood cultures appear to be sterilized after even 1 or 2 doses of antibiotics, emphasizing the importance of obtaining cultures before initiating antibiotic therapy. 30. If the laboratory is alerted to the possibility of anthrax, biochemical testing and review of colonial morphology can provide a preliminary diagnosis within 12 to 24 hours after inoculation of the cultures. 31. Definitive diagnosis can be promptly confirmed by a Laboratory Response Network (LRN) laboratory. 32. If the clinical laboratory is not alerted to the possibility of anthrax, Bacillus anthracis may not be correctly identified. 33. Routine procedures typically identify a Bacillus species in a blood culture approximately 24 hours after growth, but some laboratories do not further identify Bacillus species unless specifically requested. 34. This is because the isolation of Bacillus species most often represents growth of the common contaminant Bacillus cereus. 35. Given the possibility of future anthrax attacks, it is recommended that routine clinical laboratory procedures be modified to specifically exclude Bacillus anthracis after identifying a Bacillus species bacteremia unless there are compelling reasons not to do so. 36. If Bacillus anthracis cannot be excluded, the isolate should be transferred to an LRN laboratory. 37. Sputum culture and Gram stain are unlikely to be diagnostic of inhalational anthrax due to the frequent lack of a pneumonic process. 38. Gram stain of sputum was reported positive in only one case of inhalational anthrax in the 2001 series. 39. If cutaneous anthrax is suspected, a Gram stain and culture of vesicular fluid should be obtained. 40. If the Gram stain is negative or the patient is already taking antibiotics, a punch biopsy should be performed, and specimens sent to a laboratory capable of immunohistochemical staining or polymerase chain reaction assays. 41. Blood cultures should be obtained, and antibiotics should be initiated pending confirmation of the diagnosis of inhalational or cutaneous anthrax. 42. Nasal swabs were obtained in some individuals believed to be at risk of inhalational anthrax following the 2001 attacks. 43. 44. It is not known how quickly antibiotics render spore recovery on nasal swab tests impossible. 45. One patient who died from inhalational anthrax had a negative nasal swab. 46. The CDC advised in the fall of 2001 that the nasal swab should not be used as a clinical diagnostic test. 47. If obtained for epidemiological purposes, nasal swabs should be interpreted with caution.
